source.title: The Art of War
source.attribution: Sun Tzu, The Art of War (trans. Lionel Giles), Standard Ebooks, public domain

cards.title: Most contests are decided by the preparation done beforehand
cards.body:
Sun Tzu noticed that winners do most of their winning before anything starts. They compare strengths, study the ground and think through what could go wrong, while losers count on improvising once things are underway.

The same applies to a pitch, a salary conversation or a product launch. The decisive work happens in the quiet hours before: researching the other side, rehearsing likely objections, checking the numbers. Walk in prepared and the meeting confirms work you have already done instead of becoming a gamble.
cards.quote: Now the general who wins a battle makes many calculations in his temple ere the battle is fought. The general who loses a battle makes but few calculations beforehand.
cards.apply_it: Before your next important meeting, write down the three objections you most expect and a short answer to each.

quiz.question: According to Sun Tzu, what separates winning generals from losing ones?
options: Many calculations made before the battle
quiz.explanation: Sun Tzu tied victory to the amount of thinking done before the battle, not to improvising during it.

cards.title: The best victory is the one that needs no fight
cards.body:
Sun Tzu ranked winning without battle above winning every battle. Even a fight you win costs time, money, energy and goodwill, and it leaves an opponent who may come back for revenge.

In business and at work this means looking for outcomes the other side can accept. A negotiation that leaves your counterpart humiliated often produces a deal they resent and quietly undermine. Settling a dispute with a smart offer, a better alternative or a shared interest avoids the costs of open conflict and keeps the relationship usable next time.
cards.quote: Hence to fight and conquer in all your battles is not supreme excellence; supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting.
cards.apply_it: Pick one disagreement you are in. What could you offer that gives the other side something they want while you still get what you need?

quiz.question: Why did Sun Tzu rank winning without fighting above winning every battle?
options: Because even won battles carry heavy costs
Because fighting is always morally wrong
Because fighting is too slow to be useful
quiz.explanation: Open conflict drains resources and goodwill even for the winner, so the cheapest victory is the best one.

cards.title: Know the other side and know yourself, or expect mixed results
cards.body:
Sun Tzu's most quoted line has two halves, and most people remember only one. Studying a competitor, a client or a hiring manager is not enough; you also need an honest view of your own strengths, gaps and limits.

Know only yourself and you will win some and lose some without knowing why. Know neither and you are guessing. Before a job interview, a sales call or a market entry, research the other side carefully, then just as carefully list where you are strong and where you are exposed.
cards.quote: If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will also suffer a defeat.
cards.apply_it: Before your next big conversation, write two lists: what the other side most wants, and your own two biggest weak spots in this situation.

quiz.question: What happens, according to Sun Tzu, if you know yourself but not the enemy?
options: You win some and suffer defeats too
quiz.explanation: Self-knowledge alone gives mixed results; you need to understand the other side as well.

cards.title: Make yourself hard to beat first, then wait for openings
cards.body:
Sun Tzu split success into two parts. Not losing is in your own hands; the chance to win usually comes from outside, often from someone else's mistake. So good generals secured their position first and then watched for the opening.

In a career this means building what you control: savings to cover a few months, skills that stay in demand, a solid reputation and a network. None of that guarantees a big break, but it keeps a setback from sinking you and lets you move quickly when a good opportunity appears.
cards.quote: To secure ourselves against defeat lies in our own hands, but the opportunity of defeating the enemy is provided by the enemy himself.
cards.apply_it: Name one thing you can do this week that makes you harder to knock over, such as adding to savings, updating your CV or sharpening a key skill.

quiz.question: Which part of victory did Sun Tzu say lies in our own hands?
quiz.explanation: Protecting yourself from defeat is within your control; the opening to win is usually offered by the other side.

cards.title: Long, drawn-out conflicts drain everyone involved
cards.body:
Sun Tzu warned that no state has ever gained from a long war. Supplies run down, morale sags, and even the eventual winner is weaker than before.

Modern versions are everywhere: a lawsuit that drags on for years, a price war with a rival, a cold feud with a colleague, a failing project nobody will stop. Each month quietly eats money, attention and energy. When you enter a conflict, decide in advance what a good result looks like and when you will settle, change course or walk away.
cards.quote: There is no instance of a country having benefited from prolonged warfare.
cards.apply_it: Think of a dispute or project that has dragged on. Set a date by which you will either resolve it or step away.

quiz.question: What was Sun Tzu's view of prolonged warfare?
options: It wears down the enemy and so pays off
It is fine if the cause is just
No country has ever benefited from it
It is the surest path to victory
quiz.explanation: Long conflicts drain resources on all sides, so even the winner comes out weaker.

cards.title: Never make a big move just because you are angry
cards.body:
Sun Tzu told rulers and generals never to start a fight out of irritation or wounded pride. Anger fades and moods recover, he noted, but a ruined position cannot be undone.

The same trap shows up in the furious reply to a client, the resignation sent after one bad meeting, or the public post written in a temper. The feeling is temporary; the consequences may not be. Act only when there is a real gain to be had, and give strong emotions time to cool before you commit to anything you cannot take back.
cards.quote: No ruler should put troops into the field merely to gratify his own spleen; no general should fight a battle simply out of pique.
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel the urge to send an angry message, save it as a draft and reread it tomorrow before deciding.

quiz.question: Why did Sun Tzu warn against fighting out of anger?
options: Anger is a sign of weak leadership only
Anger passes, but the damage from a rash battle may be permanent
quiz.explanation: Moods change and recover, but a destroyed position or relationship may never come back.

cards.title: Don't repeat last year's winning move by default
cards.body:
Sun Tzu compared good strategy to water, which takes whatever shape the ground gives it and flows around high points toward low ones. A tactic that won once should not become a habit, because the next situation will be different.

Companies fall into this when they keep reusing the campaign, product or pricing that worked years ago. People do it when they handle every manager or negotiation the same way. Look at the conditions in front of you, avoid where the other side is strongest, and aim your effort where they are thin.
cards.quote: Do not repeat the tactics which have gained you one victory, but let your methods be regulated by the infinite variety of circumstances.
cards.apply_it: Pick one routine approach at work. Ask: would I still choose this method if I were starting fresh today?

quiz.question: What image did Sun Tzu use for adapting tactics to circumstances?
quiz.explanation: Water changes shape to fit the ground, just as tactics should fit each new situation.

cards.title: Good leaders combine wisdom, sincerity, kindness, courage and firmness
cards.body:
Among the five factors Sun Tzu says decide every contest is the commander, whom he defines by five virtues: wisdom, sincerity, benevolence, courage and strictness.

The list is useful because the qualities balance each other. Kindness without firmness becomes weakness; firmness without kindness becomes harshness. Courage without wisdom is recklessness. Whether you lead a business, a project or a family, it is worth asking which of the five you lean on and which you neglect. Most leaders are strong in two or three and need deliberate work on the rest.
cards.quote: The Commander stands for the virtues of wisdom, sincerity, benevolence, courage and strictness.
cards.apply_it: Rate yourself from 1 to 5 on each of the five virtues. Pick your lowest and choose one small way to practise it this week.

quiz.question: Which list matches the five virtues of a commander in The Art of War?
options: Strength, size, age, noble birth, fame
quiz.explanation: Sun Tzu defines the commander by wisdom, sincerity, benevolence, courage and strictness.

cards.title: Reward and correct people consistently, not by mood
cards.body:
When Sun Tzu compares two armies to predict who will win, one of his seven questions is which side is more constant in reward and punishment. People perform best when they know that good work will be recognised and that rules apply to everyone, every time.

In a workplace, inconsistency is corrosive. If praise depends on the manager's mood, or rules are bent for favourites, people stop trying and start guessing. Clear standards, applied the same way to everyone, build trust and effort.
cards.quote: In which army is there the greater constancy both in reward and punishment?
cards.apply_it: Think of a rule or reward in your team or home. Is it applied the same way to everyone? Fix one inconsistency.

quiz.question: Which question does Sun Tzu use to compare two armies?
options: Which side has the most colourful banners
Which side is more constant in reward and punishment
Which side has the oldest general
Which side has the most allies abroad
quiz.explanation: Constancy in reward and punishment is one of his seven considerations for forecasting victory.

cards.title: Compete where rivals are weak, not where they are strongest
cards.body:
Sun Tzu compares strategy to water, which flows away from high ground and towards low places. In the same way, he says, avoid what is strong and strike at what is weak.

For a small business, this means not copying the biggest competitor head-on with fewer resources. Look for the customers they serve badly, the areas they ignore, or the service they are too big to offer. In a job search or negotiation, lead with your strengths where others are thin. Effort spent where resistance is lowest goes furthest.
cards.quote: So in war, the way is to avoid what is strong and to strike at what is weak.
cards.apply_it: Name one area where a big competitor serves customers poorly. Could you do that one thing much better?

quiz.question: What does Sun Tzu's comparison of strategy to water teach?
options: Always meet the strongest rival head-on
Stay still and never change course
Avoid what is strong and strike at what is weak
quiz.explanation: Water flows away from high places to low ones; strategy should likewise avoid strength and target weakness.

cards.title: Choose your battles: knowing when not to fight is a skill
cards.body:
The first of Sun Tzu's five essentials for victory is simple: the winner knows when to fight and when not to.

Many of us waste energy on every argument, rival or slight. Not every critic needs an answer, and not every competitor's move needs a response. Before engaging, ask whether this fight matters to your goals, whether you can win it, and what it will cost. Saving your energy for the few contests that truly count makes you far more effective when they come.
cards.quote: He will win who knows when to fight and when not to fight.
cards.apply_it: List three conflicts or disputes you're currently in. Drop the one that matters least to your real goals.

quiz.question: What is the first of Sun Tzu's five essentials for victory?
options: Knowing when to fight and when not to fight
quiz.explanation: He says the one who knows when to fight and when not to fight will win.

cards.title: A team wins when the same spirit runs through every level
cards.body:
Sun Tzu says victory goes to the army animated by the same spirit throughout all its ranks. When generals, officers and soldiers share the same purpose, orders are understood and effort pulls in one direction.

Organisations often fail not from lack of talent but from a gap between what leaders say and what front-line staff believe. Explain the 'why' behind goals, listen to people at every level, and make sure rewards match the stated mission. Shared purpose turns a group into a team.
cards.quote: He will win whose army is animated by the same spirit throughout all its ranks.
cards.apply_it: Ask someone at a different level of your organisation what they think the main goal is. Compare it with yours.

quiz.question: Which army will win, according to Sun Tzu?
options: The one with the same spirit throughout all its ranks
The one whose leaders keep plans from the troops
The one with the most expensive equipment
The one that marches the furthest
quiz.explanation: Shared spirit across every rank is one of his five essentials for victory.

cards.title: Don't give orders from afar that the people on the ground can't carry out
cards.body:
Sun Tzu lists ways a ruler can harm his own army. The first is ordering it to advance or retreat without knowing that it cannot obey, which he calls 'hobbling the army'.

The modern version is the manager who sets deadlines, targets or procedures without understanding the realities of the work. Those orders waste effort and erode trust. If you lead, ask the people doing the job what is possible before deciding, and give them room to adapt to conditions you can't see.
cards.quote: By commanding the army to advance or to retreat, being ignorant of the fact that it cannot obey. This is called hobbling the army.
cards.apply_it: Before setting your next deadline or target for others, ask the people doing the work what is realistic.

quiz.question: What does Sun Tzu call it when a ruler gives orders the army cannot obey?
quiz.explanation: Commanding an advance or retreat without knowing the army cannot obey is called hobbling the army.

cards.title: Real skill often looks unremarkable because it avoids mistakes
cards.body:
Sun Tzu says the truly skilled fighter wins easily, so his victories earn no reputation for brilliance or courage. He wins by making no mistakes, which means he only fights opponents who have already put themselves in a losing position.

In work, the most competent people often look quiet: their projects run on time, their accounts are in order, and crises rarely happen. Dramatic rescues get praised, but steady avoidance of errors is the deeper skill. Value it in yourself and in others.
cards.quote: He wins his battles by making no mistakes.
cards.apply_it: List the three most common mistakes in your work. Create a simple checklist to prevent one of them.

quiz.question: How does the skilled fighter win, according to Sun Tzu?
options: By fighting the strongest enemy first
quiz.explanation: He says the skilled fighter wins by making no mistakes, so his victories look easy.

cards.title: A few basic moves, combined well, create endless options
cards.body:
Sun Tzu points out that there are only five musical notes, five primary colours and five basic tastes, yet their combinations are more than anyone could ever hear, see or taste. In battle there are only two basic methods, direct and indirect, but combined they produce endless manoeuvres.

Creativity in business rarely needs exotic ingredients. A new product, service or marketing idea often comes from combining familiar elements in a fresh way. When you feel stuck, list your basic building blocks and try new combinations.
cards.quote: In battle, there are not more than two methods of attack⁠—the direct and the indirect; yet these two in combination give rise to an endless series of manoeuvres.
cards.apply_it: Write down five things your business or skill set already includes. Combine any two into one new offer or idea.

quiz.question: What point does Sun Tzu make with musical notes, colours and tastes?
options: Only experts can create anything new
There are too many options to choose from
A few basic elements can combine into endless variations
quiz.explanation: Just as five notes make endless melodies, two methods of attack combine into endless manoeuvres.

cards.title: Build strength from the team's combined energy, not individual heroes
cards.body:
Sun Tzu says the clever commander looks to the effect of combined energy and does not demand too much from individuals. He picks the right people and puts them where the situation carries them forward, like round stones rolling downhill.

Organisations that rely on one star employee or one overworked founder are fragile. Better results come from setting up conditions such as clear roles, good timing and momentum that let ordinary people achieve a lot together, without burning anyone out.
cards.quote: The clever combatant looks to the effect of combined energy, and does not require too much from individuals.
cards.apply_it: Is someone in your team, maybe you, carrying too much? Move one of their tasks to a shared system or another person.

quiz.question: What does the clever combatant rely on, according to Sun Tzu?
options: The heroism of one outstanding person
quiz.explanation: He looks to combined energy and does not require too much from individuals.

cards.title: Arrive first and fresh; rushing in late leaves you drained
cards.body:
Sun Tzu observes that whoever reaches the battlefield first and waits will be fresh for the fight, while whoever arrives second and has to hurry will arrive exhausted.

The same is true of meetings, exams, interviews and negotiations. Arriving early, having read the papers and settled your mind, gives you calm and control. Rushing in late, still catching your breath, puts you on the back foot before anything begins. Small habits of getting there first can change the outcome.
cards.quote: Whoever is first in the field and awaits the coming of the enemy, will be fresh for the fight; whoever is second in the field and has to hasten to battle will arrive exhausted.
cards.apply_it: For your next important meeting or appointment, plan to arrive 15 minutes early with your notes already reviewed.

quiz.question: What advantage does arriving first give, according to Sun Tzu?
options: You are fresh, while the latecomer arrives exhausted
You can skip the fight entirely
quiz.explanation: The first to arrive waits fresh; the one who hurries in second arrives exhausted.

cards.title: Try to be strong everywhere and you will be weak everywhere
cards.body:
Sun Tzu explains that if an enemy strengthens his front, he weakens his rear; if he strengthens his left, he weakens his right. If he sends reinforcements everywhere, he is weak everywhere.

Limited time and money work the same way. A small business that tries to serve every customer, or a person who chases every goal at once, spreads resources so thin that nothing gets enough. Choose a few priorities and concentrate on them, accepting that other areas will be thinner for now.
cards.quote: If he sends reinforcements everywhere, he will everywhere be weak.
cards.apply_it: List everything you're currently trying to improve. Pick the top two and pause the rest for a month.

quiz.question: What happens when you reinforce every position, according to Sun Tzu?
quiz.explanation: Spreading strength to every point leaves you weak at every point.

cards.title: Racing to grab an advantage can leave most of your strength behind
cards.body:
Sun Tzu warns against forced marches to seize an advantage. If an army marches day and night at double speed, the strongest arrive first, the tired fall behind, and only a tenth of the force reaches its goal.

People do the same to themselves: working through nights to hit a deadline, skipping meals and sleep to win a contract. You may arrive first, but with little left. Pushing occasionally is fine, but a pace you can sustain usually gets more of you to the finish line in good shape.
cards.quote: The stronger men will be in front, the jaded ones will fall behind, and on this plan only one-tenth of your army will reach its destination.
cards.apply_it: Look at your schedule for the next two weeks. Remove or postpone one commitment that would require working through the night.

quiz.question: What happens to an army forced to march day and night to grab an advantage?
options: It grows stronger on the way
The enemy surrenders before it arrives
Only a small fraction reaches the destination
quiz.explanation: Sun Tzu says the jaded fall behind and only one-tenth of the army reaches its goal.

cards.title: When entering new territory, use local guides
cards.body:
Sun Tzu says an army cannot make use of the natural advantages of the land unless it uses local guides. Maps and plans are not enough; you need people who know the ground.

This is practical advice for anyone moving into a new market, city or industry. Before launching a product in a new town or starting a new job, talk to people who already know how things work there: customers, suppliers, long-serving staff. Their local knowledge can save you from costly mistakes that look obvious only in hindsight.
cards.quote: We shall be unable to turn natural advantage to account unless we make use of local guides.
cards.apply_it: Before your next move into something new, find one person who already knows that ground well and ask them what outsiders get wrong.

quiz.question: What does Sun Tzu say an army needs to use the natural advantages of the land?
quiz.explanation: He says you cannot turn natural advantages to account without using local guides.

cards.title: Do your hardest work when your energy is highest
cards.body:
Sun Tzu notes that a soldier's spirit is keenest in the morning, begins to flag by noon, and by evening his mind is only on returning to camp. He calls the use of this knowledge 'the art of studying moods'.

Your own energy also rises and falls through the day. Many people think most clearly in the morning; others peak later. Notice your pattern and protect your best hours for demanding work like planning, writing or difficult conversations. Save routine tasks for when your spirit naturally dips.
cards.quote: Now a soldier's spirit is keenest in the morning; by noonday it has begun to flag; and in the evening, his mind is bent only on returning to camp.
cards.apply_it: For three days, note when you feel sharpest. Then schedule your most important task for that time.

quiz.question: When does Sun Tzu say a soldier's spirit is keenest?
quiz.explanation: He says spirit is keenest in the morning, flags by noon, and by evening turns to going home.

cards.title: Leave the other side a way out
cards.body:
Sun Tzu advises that when you surround an army, you should leave an outlet free and not press a desperate enemy too hard. People with no way out fight hardest.

In negotiations, family arguments and workplace disputes, backing someone into a corner, publicly humiliating them, or demanding total surrender usually makes them dig in. Offer a face-saving path: a compromise, a private conversation, a way to agree without looking defeated. You are more likely to get what you need, and keep the relationship.
cards.quote: When you surround an army, leave an outlet free. Do not press a desperate foe too hard.
cards.apply_it: In your next disagreement, offer the other person a way to agree that lets them keep their dignity.

quiz.question: What does Sun Tzu advise when you have surrounded an army?
quiz.explanation: He says to leave an outlet and not press a desperate foe too hard, because cornered people fight hardest.

cards.title: Don't swallow the bait
cards.body:
Among Sun Tzu's rules for manoeuvring is a blunt warning against taking whatever tempting offer an opponent dangles in front of you. Elsewhere he explains that a clever commander uses such baits to draw an enemy where he wants him.

Modern bait comes as 'too good to be true' investment returns, free gifts that lock you into contracts, or a low opening price that hides expensive extras. When an offer seems unusually generous, ask what the other side gains if you accept, and what you would be committing to.
cards.quote: Do not swallow bait offered by the enemy.
cards.apply_it: For the next deal or offer that excites you, ask: 'What does the other side gain if I say yes?' before deciding.

quiz.question: What does Sun Tzu warn against in his rules for manoeuvring?
options: Swallowing bait offered by the enemy
quiz.explanation: He warns directly: do not swallow bait offered by the enemy.

cards.title: Watch for the five faults that ruin leaders
cards.body:
Sun Tzu names five dangerous faults in a general: recklessness, which leads to destruction; cowardice, which leads to capture; a hot temper that can be provoked by insults; a sense of honour so touchy it can be shamed; and over-concern for his people, which leaves him worried and easily manipulated.

Some of these sound like virtues, which is what makes them dangerous. Caring and pride are good in moderation, but an opponent can exploit any of them. Sun Tzu urges leaders to reflect on these faults regularly.
cards.quote: When an army is overthrown and its leader slain, the cause will surely be found among these five dangerous faults. Let them be a subject of meditation.
cards.apply_it: Which of the five faults are you most prone to? Write down one situation where it has cost you, and how you would handle it now.

quiz.question: Which of these is one of the five dangerous faults Sun Tzu names?
options: A hasty temper that can be provoked by insults
quiz.explanation: His five faults are recklessness, cowardice, a hasty temper, touchy honour and over-solicitude for one's men.

cards.title: Watch what people do, not just what they say
cards.body:
Sun Tzu teaches commanders to read signs. One example: humble words combined with increased preparations mean the enemy is about to advance, while loud threats and aggressive moves may signal a retreat.

In business and negotiation, words and actions often point in different directions. A supplier who is very polite but quietly lining up other customers, or a rival making loud threats while cutting costs, is telling you something. Pay attention to the gap between what is said and what is being done.
cards.quote: Humble words and increased preparations are signs that the enemy is about to advance.
cards.locator: IX. The Army on the March ¶24
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you're negotiating with. List what they've said and, separately, what they've done. Do the two match?

quiz.question: What does Sun Tzu say humble words combined with increased preparations signal?
options: The enemy is about to advance
The enemy is running out of food
The enemy has lost its general
quiz.explanation: Humble words plus increased preparations are a sign the enemy is about to advance.

cards.title: A friendly offer with no firm commitment deserves suspicion
cards.body:
Sun Tzu warns that peace proposals not backed by a sworn agreement indicate a plot. Warm words without commitment may be a way to buy time or lower your guard.

In business, verbal promises, vague partnership talk and handshake deals with no written terms can leave you exposed. That doesn't mean everyone is lying. But when something matters, ask for the commitment to be made concrete: a written agreement, a deposit, a date. People who mean it rarely object.
cards.quote: Peace proposals unaccompanied by a sworn covenant indicate a plot.
cards.locator: IX. The Army on the March ¶26
cards.apply_it: Is there a promise someone made you that isn't written down? Politely ask to confirm the key terms in writing.

quiz.question: What does Sun Tzu say about peace proposals without a sworn covenant?
options: They mean the enemy is defeated
They are the best kind of agreement
quiz.explanation: He says peace proposals unaccompanied by a sworn covenant indicate a plot.

cards.title: Never take your competition lightly
cards.body:
Sun Tzu warns that whoever exercises no forethought and makes light of his opponents is sure to be captured by them.

Successful businesses often fall this way: they dismiss a small new rival, a cheaper product or a change in customer habits until it is too late. The same happens to students who underrate an exam or athletes who underrate an opponent. Respecting the competition, studying what they do well and preparing properly are signs of strength, not fear.
cards.quote: He who exercises no forethought but makes light of his opponents is sure to be captured by them.
cards.locator: IX. The Army on the March ¶41
cards.apply_it: Name one competitor or challenge you've been dismissing. Spend 20 minutes studying what they do well.

quiz.question: What happens to one who makes light of his opponents, according to Sun Tzu?
options: He is sure to be captured by them
quiz.explanation: Sun Tzu says one who exercises no forethought and makes light of opponents will be captured.

cards.title: Win people's trust first, then hold them to high standards
cards.body:
Sun Tzu notes that if soldiers are punished before they feel attached to their leader, they will resist; but if they are attached and discipline is never enforced, they are also useless. His answer: treat people first with humanity, and keep them in order with firm discipline.

Good managers, teachers and parents do both. Build a real relationship and show you care, so that feedback is heard. Then keep clear standards and follow through, so the care doesn't turn into indulgence.
cards.quote: Therefore soldiers must be treated in the first instance with humanity, but kept under control by means of iron discipline.
cards.locator: IX. The Army on the March ¶43
cards.apply_it: With someone you supervise or mentor, check: have you built enough trust for honest feedback? Do you follow through on standards?

quiz.question: What does Sun Tzu say about treating soldiers?
options: First with humanity, then kept in order by firm discipline
Only with strict punishments from day one
Only with kindness and no rules
With indifference, so they stay independent
quiz.explanation: He says to treat soldiers first with humanity but keep them under control with iron discipline.

cards.title: Unclear orders and fuzzy roles lead to chaos
cards.body:
Among the disasters Sun Tzu blames on the leader rather than on bad luck is 'disorganization'. It happens when the leader is weak, orders are not clear, no one has fixed duties and things are done in a careless, haphazard way.

Many teams feel busy but get little done for exactly this reason. Everyone assumes someone else is handling a task, or different people hear different instructions. Clear goals, named owners for each task and simple written instructions prevent much of the confusion.
cards.quote: when his orders are not clear and distinct; when there are no fixed duties assigned to officers and men, and the ranks are formed in a slovenly haphazard manner, the result is utter disorganization.
cards.apply_it: For your current main project, write each task next to the name of the one person responsible for it.

quiz.question: According to Sun Tzu, what causes utter disorganisation in an army?
options: Unclear orders and no fixed duties
quiz.explanation: He says unclear orders, no fixed duties and haphazard ranks lead to utter disorganization.

cards.title: Even rivals help each other when they are in the same boat
cards.body:
Sun Tzu points out that the people of Wu and Yüeh were enemies, yet if they crossed a river in the same boat and a storm hit, they would help each other like a left hand helping the right.

A shared threat or shared goal can unite people who normally compete: neighbouring shop owners facing a new mall, departments facing a crisis, family members who disagree but need to care for a parent. When cooperation feels impossible, look for the 'storm' you both face and start from there.
cards.quote: if they are crossing a river in the same boat and are caught by a storm, they will come to each other's assistance just as the left hand helps the right.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you clash with. Name one challenge you both face, and suggest working on it together.

quiz.question: What brings the enemies of Wu and Yüeh together in Sun Tzu's example?
options: A peace treaty signed by their kings
Being caught by a storm in the same boat
quiz.explanation: A shared danger in the same boat makes even enemies help each other.
